title: India Maps 27 Arunachal Pradesh Sites With Official Names to Counter China
excerpt: The Ministry of Home Affairs formally standardized strategic locations including Thag La and Dzo La on Survey of India maps, pushing back against Beijing's systematic renaming campaign.
body:
• India has officially standardized 27 geographical sites in Arunachal Pradesh on Survey of India maps, including strategic passes like Thag La and Dzo La, in a coordinated move with the state government to counter China's repeated renaming attempts.
  • The cartographic update comes amid social media reports of a Chinese incursion in the state, which Chief Minister Pema Khandu and the Indian Army have both denied as baseless.
  • China has renamed places in Arunachal Pradesh six times since 2017 — covering more than 90 locations — as part of what analysts call a "cartographic war" to assert its claim over the region it calls "Zangnan."

India has formally mapped 27 places and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh on official Survey of India maps, the Ministry of Home Affairs announced on Friday, in what amounts to a direct counter to China's systematic renaming of locations in the northeastern state.

The initiative, carried out in consultation with the Government of Arunachal Pradesh, standardizes the names of 21 land areas, four mountain passes, one lake, and one memorial — including strategically significant sites like Longju, Thag La, and Dzo La — on the country's official cartographic records.

What Was Named

According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, the 27 locations include land areas such as Longju, Maja, Bisa, Bara Kundun, Chhota Kundun, Dhan Bari, Pritnagar, Buddhamandir, Jairampur, Jaswant Garh, Shivaji Nagar, and Kamlang Nagar. Four passes — Dzo La, Riza La, Pukur La, and Thag La — were also formalized, along with a lake called Sambho Sarovar and the Sher-e-Thapa Memorial.

Several of these names carry historical weight. Thag La ridge was the site of the first major engagement of the 1962 Sino-Indian war. Jaswant Garh is named after Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat, who held a post against Chinese forces during that conflict and was posthumously awarded the Maha Vir Chakra.

Countering the Map War

China has systematically renamed locations in Arunachal Pradesh six times since 2017, issuing lists through its Ministry of Civil Affairs covering more than 90 sites it claims as part of "Zangnan" — its Chinese name for what it considers South Tibet. The most recent list, published in May 2025, covered 27 locations including mountains, rivers, residential areas, and a mountain pass.

India has rejected every such attempt. External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal has called the efforts "vain and preposterous," stating that "creative naming will not alter the undeniable reality that Arunachal Pradesh was, is, and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of India."

"Identifying them formally on the Survey of India map of Arunachal Pradesh is aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large."

— Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India

Incursion Reports Denied

The mapping announcement coincides with social media reports alleging a Chinese incursion along the Line of Actual Control in Arunachal Pradesh. Chief Minister Pema Khandu dismissed the reports on Friday, saying he would speak to both local tribal leaders and the Indian Army but did not believe an incursion had taken place.

"We don't think there was an incursion as the Indian Army personnel are deployed and maintaining the territory," Khandu said.

The Indian Army separately called the reports "incorrect and without any basis," reaffirming that border security remains intact. Last month, Arunachal Pradesh Home Minister Mama Natung similarly dismissed encroachment claims as "just rumours."

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

The India-China border dispute remains one of the most closely watched geopolitical flashpoints for the Indian diaspora. Arunachal Pradesh sits at the eastern end of the 3,488-kilometer Line of Actual Control, and any escalation echoes through diplomatic and community channels worldwide. India's decision to proactively standardize place names — rather than simply rejecting Chinese ones — represents a more assertive posture in the long-running cartographic contest.
